mappings.note: The third law is handed to the student in the stem; what must be supplied is a = F/m - why the light needle swings and the heavy magnet does not (LO-6). LO-8 is second because the equal-force premise is the thing being reconciled, not the thing being recalled.
Verbatim LO-61 - a force needs magnitude and direction. Nothing about balance or about motion, so neither LO-62 nor LO-64.
LO-7's second clause is 'Define SI unit of force', the only home for unit questions in this frame. Not LO-6 - no statement of the law is wanted.
Canonical balanced-forces identification. The rope stays at rest so nothing is inferred from a velocity change (not LO-64), and no explanation beyond the label is demanded (not LO-65).

Resultant of like-directed forces - an unbalanced-force identification with trivial arithmetic. Only a magnitude is asked, so LO-61 is not needed; O5 and O6 demand a direction and therefore do carry it.
Opposing forces must be differenced (LO-62) and the option set cannot be resolved without committing to a direction (LO-61). That direction requirement is exactly what separates this from O4.
Identical demand to O5 in worded rather than diagrammed form. Mapped to the same pair deliberately rather than split on presentation.

Statements 1 and 2 are LO-64 (a force changes the state of motion), with statement 2 needing force as a directed quantity (LO-61). Statement 3, change of shape, has no outcome anywhere in this frame - flagged as a partial fit.
Names friction as the force opposing the push on a stationary box - LO-63 at identification level. Not LO-62: the question asks which force, not whether the pair balances.

Ranks four surfaces by how much friction each supplies and hence how far the coins travel. LO-63 is the only friction outcome in the frame; there is none for friction depending on the nature of the surfaces.

Each table row is a balanced/unbalanced judgement (LO-62) and the winning criterion is zero net force with the block already moving (LO-64) - Block Y is balanced too but at rest, which is the trap. No graph, so no C2.1 or C8.1.

The historical claim being attributed is precisely the first law (LO-5), and the thought experiment is defined by removing friction (LO-63). Newton is the distractor, so the graded content is the law's statement, not its application.

The assertion is LO-64 verbatim; the reason that must be validated is that the balancing partner is friction (LO-63). The assertion-reason format makes the friction clause load-bearing, which is why it is cited and not LO-64 alone.
Four statements about the first law including the inertia alias. Statement 4 brushes LO-64, but the item is scored on knowing the law, so LO-5 alone.
Everyday event explained by the second law via increased stopping time. Distractor (A) is a plausible second-law-sounding wrong answer, so the discrimination is still LO-6 and not LO-8.

Runs from physics to representation: zero net force implies constant velocity (LO-64) and the student must produce the corresponding graph shape (C8.1). No graph is supplied to read, which is why C8.1 and not C2.1.
Recognition of the second law's algebraic form with no substitution. LO-7 is for producing a value from that expression; nothing is computed here.

A supplied table of initial velocity and net force is read against a stated graph shape - analysing a given representation (C2.1) using the zero-net-force criterion (LO-64). Car P, zero force but at rest, is the trap. O15 goes the other way, physics to graph, and so takes C8.1.
Definition of the SI unit of force, the tail clause of LO-7. The 1 kg / 1 m s-2 substitution is the definition itself, not a free-standing calculation.
Only the force-newton row falls inside this frame, via LO-7's SI-unit clause. Kilogram, m/s and m/s^2 belong to the kinematics unit and have no outcome here - flagged as a partial fit.
The base case of the numerical family: one substitution into F = ma with both inputs given and force as the unknown. Nothing else is graded.
A near-duplicate of O14 in the bank. Mapped to the same pair deliberately rather than inventing a distinction between asking for the 'principle' and asking for the 'purpose'.
Same everyday-application-of-the-second-law outcome as O14 and O21; the assertion-reason form only flips the direction of the time change, which does not move the outcome.
Differs from the base numerical O20 by exactly one graded step: friction must be subtracted before F = ma is applied, so LO-63 joins LO-7.
A given velocity-time graph is read (C2.1) and converted to a net-force verdict (LO-64). No number is produced, so unlike N11 there is no LO-7.
